summary: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 could previously attach only a single tag, and only for AS-external and NSSA prefixes. With flexible encodings in newer OSPF extensions, this RFC lets routers advertise administrative tags for prefixes more generally.

eli5.summary: Routers can stick labels on networks. Before, only a few networks could get one label. Now many more can have labels.

questions: how to tag prefixes in ospf
subtitle: Let routers label networks with multiple administrative tags for policy and optimization.

tldr.problem: OSPF routers could previously associate only a single tag with prefixes, and only for routes from other AS or from not-so-stubby areas, limiting the policy and optimization options available to network operators.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9825 defines an Administrative Tag Sub-TLV that carries one or more 32-bit unsigned integer tags for any prefix type in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, using the flexible encoding mechanisms already defined in RFC 7684 and RFC 8362.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now tag any prefix with multiple labels to control redistribution policy, prioritize certain routes, select prefixes for fast reroute protection, and implement many other routing policies consistently across their networks.

today: RFC 9825 is a Proposed Standard. It enables OSPF routers to advertise multiple administrative tags on any prefix type, supporting routing policies that were previously limited to external and NSSA routes. Deployment depends on router vendor implementation, with initial focus on redistribution control and fast reroute optimization.

sections.title: The Problem with One Tag
sections.content:
In the original OSPF specification, routers could attach a single tag to routes that came from outside the autonomous system (AS) or from not-so-stubby areas (NSSAs). These tags were useful for policy decisions: a router could say, for example, "if this route has tag 100, send it to BGP; if it has tag 200, drop it." But this mechanism had limitations.

First, only AS-external and NSSA routes could carry tags; routes learned from other routers in the same OSPF domain had no way to be labeled. Second, each route could carry only one tag, even though operators often wanted to apply multiple independent policies. Network operators needed a way to label any prefix with multiple tags, similar to the mechanism already deployed in IS-IS.
sections.eli5: The old OSPF could only put one sticker on certain types of packages, and not on others. Network managers wanted to put many stickers on any package, so they could route it based on multiple rules at once.

sections.title: The Administrative Tag Sub-TLV
sections.content:
RFC 9825 defines a new sub-TLV (a sub-component of OSPF's link state advertisements) called the Administrative Tag Sub-TLV. It carries a list of one or more 32-bit unsigned integers that represent tags.

The sub-TLV has a simple structure: a type field (which varies depending on the OSPF version and prefix type), a length field that indicates how many bytes follow (always a multiple of 4, since each tag is 4 bytes), and then the tag values themselves. The RFC specifies three type values: 13 for OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLVs, 39 for OSPFv3 Extended LSAs, and 6 for OSPFv3 SRv6 locators.

Routers MUST support at least one tag per prefix. Most routers will support multiple tags, though the exact number depends on the implementation and the local policy. Tags have no inherent meaning or ordering; each tag is simply an autonomous identifier that policies can act upon.
sections.eli5: The tag sub-TLV is like a sticky note. It says "I am a tag" (the type), how many bytes come next (the length), and then lists the numbers. Each number is a sticker you can stick on a network.

sections.title: Where Tags Appear
sections.content:
Before RFC 9825, the single tag field was hardcoded into the AS-External and NSSA LSA formats themselves. The new Administrative Tag Sub-TLV takes a different approach: it is a sub-component that plugs into the more flexible advertisement mechanisms defined in RFC 7684 (OSPFv2 Prefix/Link Attribute Advertisement) and RFC 8362 (OSPFv3 Extended Link State Advertisements).

In OSPFv2, tags attach to the Extended Prefix TLV advertised in opaque LSAs (types 9, 10, and 11). In OSPFv3, tags can appear in four places: the Inter-Area-Prefix TLV, the Intra-Area-Prefix TLV, the External-Prefix TLV in AS-External LSAs, and the External-Prefix TLV in NSSA LSAs. There is also support for tags on SRv6 locators (RFC 9513). For backward compatibility, when a router advertises the first tag on an AS-External or NSSA prefix, it SHOULD use the existing tag field in the LSA itself; additional tags use the new sub-TLV.

This flexibility means any prefix type—internal, summarized, external, or SRv6 locator—can now carry multiple tags, whereas before only external and NSSA prefixes had any tag at all.
sections.eli5: Tags used to go in special places for special routes. Now they fit into the newer, more flexible advertisement format, so any route type can have them.

sections.title: How Routers Use and Propagate Tags
sections.content:
An OSPF router that supports this RFC will advertise tags when it originates prefixes (for example, routes it learns from local interfaces, or routes it redistributes from another protocol). When a router receives prefixes with tags from its neighbors, it can use those tags in its local policies.

Area Border Routers (ABRs) act as translators between areas. When an ABR advertises a summary route into another area, the RFC recommends that it carry the tags from the contributing intra-area routes along with it, so downstream routers can apply the same policies. Similarly, when an ABR translates NSSA routes to AS-External routes, it should preserve the tags if possible. However, local policy can suppress tag propagation if needed—for example, a network operator might not want external routes leaking specific tags into an internal area.

When multiple router paths contribute to a route (equal-cost multipath), and those paths have different tags, an ABR MUST choose which tags to advertise. The RFC recommends adding tags in ascending order of the originating router's Router-ID. The number of tags an ABR propagates is limited by its implementation and its configured policies.

For aggregated or summarized routes created locally (area ranges, NSSA ranges, redistributed summaries), the RFC says tags SHOULD NOT be automatically inherited from the component routes; instead, operators SHOULD configure tags explicitly on the summary itself if needed.
sections.eli5: Routers put tags on the routes they advertise. When one router hears about a route from another, it remembers the tags. When the first router tells a neighboring area about that route, it passes the tags along—unless someone says not to. When different paths have different tags, the router picks one set to use.

sections.title: Practical Applications
sections.content:
Tags enable several important routing policies. The RFC itself mentions three main use cases, though others are possible.

First, redistribution control: a router can be configured to leak OSPF routes into BGP only if they carry a specific tag. This lets operators segment their network so that internal routes stay internal while tagged routes are advertised externally, all based on policy.

Second, convergence optimization: some prefixes are more critical than others. Operators can tag high-priority prefixes and instruct routers to install and converge on them faster, ahead of lower-priority routes.

Third, fast reroute protection: IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) and Loop-Free Alternatives (LFA) compute backup paths in case a primary link fails. Operators can tag prefixes to indicate which ones deserve protection, allowing routers to prioritize LFA computation for critical services.

Tags can also be used for traffic engineering, for VPN route isolation, and for many application-specific purposes. The RFC explicitly states that the meaning of tags is a local matter; there is no global registry of tag numbers. Two network operators might use tag 100 to mean entirely different things.
sections.eli5: Tags help routers make better decisions. One example: "Routes with tag 100 go to BGP." Another: "Tag 200 means route this fast." A third: "Tag 300 means protect this with a backup path." Each network decides what its tags mean.

sections.title: BGP-LS and the Broader Ecosystem
sections.content:
OSPF is one of several link-state routing protocols. Another important tool in the routing ecosystem is BGP-LS (Border Gateway Protocol - Link State), which lets routers advertise OSPF or IS-IS topology information via BGP. RFC 9552 defined the BGP-LS IGP Route Tag TLV (code 1153) specifically to carry administrative tags learned from IS-IS or OSPF.

RFC 9825 confirms that the OSPF tags defined here will be advertised via BGP-LS using that TLV. This means a network can use BGP-LS to export its OSPF tagging policies to external systems—for example, to a central traffic engineering controller, a path computation server, or a network-wide analytics system. These external systems can then make informed decisions about which routes to use and how to engineer traffic based on the tags visible in OSPF.
sections.eli5: BGP-LS is a system that talks about OSPF routes in a different language, so other parts of the network (like traffic controllers) can understand them. It now includes OSPF tags so the external systems see the full picture.

sections.title: Security and Management
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit about the security model. The tags themselves are less sensitive than the underlying OSPF topology; if an attacker modifies a tag, the network does not immediately break. However, if tags are used for important policies—like controlling which routes are redistributed or which prefixes get fast reroute protection—then tag integrity matters.

The RFC includes a complete YANG data model (a machine-readable schema) for configuring and monitoring OSPF administrative tags. This data model is accessed via NETCONF or RESTCONF, both of which MUST use secure transport (SSH, TLS, or QUIC) and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) provides fine-grained access control, so that only authorized network operators can change tag configurations.

The RFC identifies several sensitive data nodes: the local-prefix-admin-tags and area range admin-tags configurations are sensitive because they control which tags are advertised; the link-state database contents are sensitive because they could be used to mount denial-of-service attacks if exposed to unauthorized parties. Implementations SHOULD rate-limit logging of malformed tags (for example, tags with invalid lengths) to avoid flooding the system log.
sections.eli5: Tags are not as critical as the network topology itself, but they still matter for policy. Access to the configuration tools MUST be secured with passwords and encryption. Only trusted operators should be able to change tags.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 9825 is a Proposed Standard, approved by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) in July 2025. It has been registered with IANA: type 13 for OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLVs, type 39 for OSPFv3 Extended LSAs, and type 6 for OSPFv3 SRv6 Locator LSA sub-TLVs. The YANG module name ietf-ospf-admin-tags has also been registered.

Deployment will depend on router vendor support. Early implementations will likely focus on the core use cases: redistribution control and fast reroute prioritization. Over time, operators will find additional applications—traffic engineering, service routing, network slicing, and others. Unlike the fixed single-tag model, this extensible mechanism allows operators to adapt tagging policies to their evolving needs without waiting for IETF standards updates.
sections.eli5: The standard is official as of July 2025. Router vendors are starting to add support. Once routers understand tags, network operators can use them for many different policies.
